subtype: Stage 1: A hurt that is not spoken [Actor]
passage:
I still remember the Tuesday it started. I'm Arohi, and back then Madhuri and I had eaten lunch on the same bench since Class 6.

That day I came out of the lab late and saw her at the big table under the neem tree, laughing with the debate girls. My dabba felt heavy in my hands.

I could have walked up. I could have asked, "Hey, why didn't you wait?" But asking felt like begging, and I was too proud for that. I also couldn't just sit down and act normal, because my throat was hot.

So I sat on our bench alone and ate without tasting anything. When Madhuri waved across the courtyard, I looked at the wall like it was very interesting.

She stopped waving. Neither of us said anything that whole afternoon.

qa.q: Where was Madhuri sitting at lunch?
qa.a: She was at the big table under the neem tree, laughing with the debate girls.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when Madhuri waved?
qa.a: Arohi felt hurt and left out, but too proud to show it, so Arohi looked away instead.

qa.q: What small step could Arohi have tried that afternoon?
qa.a: Arohi could have said simply, 'I missed you at lunch today,' which names the hurt without accusing.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when Arohi looked away?
qa.a: Madhuri was probably confused and a bit stung, not knowing what had gone wrong, so she stopped waving.

grounding: A teenager feels ignored when a friend sits with others, and pride and hurt keep the teen silent and turning away.

passage:
Thursday night

Siddharth has messaged four times since Tuesday. "Hey?" "U ok?" "Did I do something?" and a meme.

I haven't replied to any of them. I read them on the lock screen so the blue ticks don't show.

Why? Because if I tell him I'm hurt that he told everyone about my audition, he'll say, "Binita, you're overreacting, it was good news!" And then I'll cry in front of him, which is worse.

This way I'm in control. I decide when we talk. Nobody can call me dramatic if I don't say anything.

But the weird part: every time my phone buzzes, I hope it's him. I kind of want him to keep trying. To realise on his own.

Is that fair? Probably not. I'm still not replying tonight.

qa.q: How many times has Siddharth messaged since Tuesday?
qa.a: Siddharth has messaged four times since Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Binita hope for while staying silent?
qa.a: Binita feels hurt and wary but secretly hopes Siddharth will keep trying and understand without being told.

qa.q: What could Binita try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Binita could reply briefly, 'I was hurt you told everyone about the audition, can we talk?', which is honest without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might Siddharth be feeling after four unanswered messages?
qa.a: Siddharth is likely confused and worried, unsure what he did and anxious that the friendship is slipping.

grounding: A teen withholds replies to feel safe and in control, fearing being called overreacting, while hoping the friend will notice and reach out first.

subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage:
Kishore, you're sulking because your friend isn't answering? Sit. Your Ritu Bua knows this one.

When I was fifteen, my best friend Chitra stopped talking to me. No fight, nothing. One Monday she just walked past my desk.

I went mad trying to understand. Was it the birthday card? The joke about her brother? I reread every letter she'd ever passed me in class, looking for clues. At night I lay awake making lists of everything I might have said.

If she had shouted at me, I'd have known where I stood. The silence was worse. It felt like the whole class had a secret and I was outside it.

After two weeks I stopped eating lunch properly. My mother noticed and asked. That was the first time I said it out loud: "Chitra doesn't want me anymore, and I don't know why."

qa.q: How old was Ritu when Chitra stopped talking to her?
qa.a: Ritu was fifteen.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during those two weeks of silence?
qa.a: She felt anxious, confused and excluded, guessing wildly and rereading old letters because she didn't know what she had done.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story?
qa.a: Telling her mother out loud what was happening, which broke the lonely guessing and let someone help her think it through.

qa.q: How might Chitra have been feeling while walking past Ritu's desk?
qa.a: Chitra was probably hurt about something she hadn't said, perhaps holding it inside and unsure how to raise it.

grounding: An elder recalls being ignored as a teen, unable to tell what she did, rereading old notes and growing anxious in the silence.

passage:
"Tenzing called again," said Pallavi didi, holding out Irfan's phone. "Fourth time today."

"Let it ring."

"What did he even do?"

"He knows what he did."

"Does he? Because he told Ammi he has no idea."

Irfan shrugged, but he didn't let go of the phone. "He left me out of the cricket team photo. On purpose."

"Did you tell him that?"

"I shouldn't have to."

Pallavi sat on his bed. "It's been six days, Irfan."

"Yeah." He stared at the screen. It felt good, a bit, that Tenzing kept trying. But he'd eaten lunch alone all week, and last night he'd almost called, then felt stupid. "If I call now, after six days, it'll look like I was wrong. It's too weird."

"It'll be weirder at twelve days," she said.

qa.q: How many days had Irfan not spoken to Tenzing?
qa.a: It had been six days.

qa.q: What is Irfan feeling about breaking the silence now?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and lonely; he likes being wanted back but thinks calling after six days would look like admitting he was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Irfan now?
qa.a: He could call Tenzing and just say what hurt, the photo, since the longer he waits the harder it will be.

qa.q: How might Tenzing be experiencing these six days?
qa.a: Tenzing seems confused and worried, calling repeatedly and telling Ammi he has no idea what he did.

grounding: A teen's silence hardens into a message, 'you should know', and though he enjoys being wanted back he grows lonelier and more embarrassed each day.

passage:
Dhruv had one bar of signal on the roof of his grandmother's house in Kangra, and a data pack that was almost gone.

For five days, Gurpreet hadn't replied. Not in class before the holidays, not now. The old Dhruv would have sent, "What's your problem??" He'd typed it twice and deleted it.

The signal flickered. He had maybe one message left before the pack ran out. He wrote it slowly, standing on tiptoe by the water tank:

"I can tell you're upset with me and I honestly don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's bad. I'm not angry. Just miss you."

He pressed send. The bar vanished. He stood in the wind for a long time, watching the valley go dark.

The next morning his grandmother's phone rang. It was Gurpreet, asking for him.

qa.q: Where was Dhruv staying?
qa.a: He was at his grandmother's house in Kangra.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he stood watching the valley after sending the message?
qa.a: He felt anxious and hopeful, unsure whether the message had arrived or whether Gurpreet would answer.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's message work better than 'What's your problem??'?
qa.a: It invited Gurpreet to speak without accusation and said he wasn't angry, which made talking feel safer than staying silent.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt reading Dhruv's message?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably felt relieved and less defensive, since the message showed care rather than blame.

grounding: With a failing signal, a teen sends a gentle message naming the silence without accusing, making it safer to talk.

passage:
The school library was nearly empty during the free period, so Maria finally said it, between the history shelves.

"Francis, I felt left out at lunch. All week. You kept sitting with the football lot."

Her heart was thumping. She'd rehearsed this for days and imagined him saying, "So? I'm allowed other friends," or laughing.

Francis looked genuinely surprised. "Oh. I didn't even think. Coach said the team should bond before the match. I thought you had your art club thing."

"That's only Wednesday."

"Right." He winced. "Sorry. I should've asked you to come. Tomorrow?"

That was it. The whole thing took less than a minute.

Walking back to class, Maria felt almost silly for how long she'd carried it. Two weeks of stomach aches for a one-minute talk.

qa.q: Where did Maria finally say it?
qa.a: She said it in the school library, between the history shelves.

qa.q: What had Maria been afraid Francis would say?
qa.a: She was afraid he'd say 'So? I'm allowed other friends' or laugh at her, which made her heart thump.

qa.q: What lesson could Maria take from this?
qa.a: Saying a hurt early and simply usually costs much less than carrying it for weeks, so next time she might speak up sooner.

qa.q: How did Francis react to hearing that Maria felt left out?
qa.a: Francis was surprised and a little sorry, having not realised, and quickly invited her to join the next day.

grounding: In a school library a teen names her hurt directly, the reply is far smaller than the fear, and both see that early honesty costs less.

passage:
Looking back, I can see what happened, but that night I couldn't have explained it to anyone. I'm Hrithik, Nazia's husband, and we'd just had our worst fight since the wedding.

It was about her parents staying another month. It got loud fast. She said I never took her side. I said something about her family I regret. Then she was crying and still talking, and I felt everything in me go white and roaring.

I couldn't find one sentence that wouldn't make it worse. So I stopped talking. I went to the balcony. When she followed me, I stared at the street.

I wasn't trying to punish her. I just had no way to handle it. It was like a circuit breaker tripping.

But from where she stood, I'd simply turned into a wall.

qa.q: What was the fight about?
qa.a: It was about Nazia's parents staying another month.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he stopped talking?
qa.a: He felt flooded and overwhelmed, with no words that seemed safe, so he shut down.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try next time he feels this overwhelmed?
qa.a: He could say, 'I'm too flooded to talk right now, I need some time, and I'll come back to this,' so the silence has a reason and an end.

qa.q: How might Nazia have experienced his silence on the balcony?
qa.a: Nazia likely felt shut out and abandoned, seeing only a wall when she wanted him to engage.

grounding: A spouse floods after a harsh argument and goes silent, not intending punishment but unable to cope with the intensity.

passage:
The staff room at Maria's school emptied at 3:40, and she stayed behind, staring at her phone.

Nine days since Hafsa had really spoken to her. Hafsa made tea, answered "fine," sat on the sofa with the television on. Maria had tried asking gently. She'd tried a long message. On Sunday she'd cried at the kitchen table, and Hafsa had just put a glass of water beside her and walked out.

Now the old feeling was back, the one from childhood, when her father would stop speaking for days: that she simply didn't matter.

She typed, "Are we even together anymore?" Deleted it. Typed, "Fine. Two can do this." Deleted that too.

When she got home that evening, she said "hi" without looking up and went straight to the bedroom. Her hands were shaking, and she could not tell anymore whether it was hurt or rage.

qa.q: How many days had it been since Hafsa had really spoken to Maria?
qa.a: It had been nine days.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she went straight to the bedroom?
qa.a: She felt invisible and powerless, with hurt turning into anger, so she went cold herself.

qa.q: How could Maria get support at this stage?
qa.a: She could talk to a trusted friend or a counsellor about the old fear this silence stirs, and tell Hafsa directly that the silence is hurting her.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Maria's cold 'hi' that evening?
qa.a: Hafsa might be confused or hurt too, or might see it as proof that talking is dangerous, which could deepen the freeze.

grounding: A partner who is shut out feels invisible, tries questions and tears, then goes cold as old fears of not mattering turn hurt to anger.

passage:
Counselling note, first joint session, 11 November.

Reena and Uma, together four years, sharing a flat. Referred by Reena's sister, who said "the house has gone silent."

Both describe a similar month. After a bad argument in October about moving cities, neither has raised it again. They talk about groceries and bills politely. They eat at different times. Reena said, "I keep waiting for her to bring it up. If I do, it'll just blow up again." Uma said almost exactly the same, a few minutes later, without hearing Reena's version.

Each admitted pride plays a part: going first feels like losing. Each also admitted fear of another fight like October's.

I pointed out that they were both waiting for the same thing. They looked at each other for the first time in the session.

Next step: a twenty-minute talk on one small topic, here, next week.

qa.q: What was the October argument about?
qa.a: It was about moving cities.

qa.q: What is Reena afraid of about bringing the subject up?
qa.a: Reena feels afraid that raising it will cause another blow-up, and proud enough that going first feels like losing.

qa.q: Why is a short talk on one small topic a sensible next step?
qa.a: It lowers the risk of another big blow-up and lets both practise speaking again, with support, before tackling moving cities.

qa.q: How might Uma feel on hearing that Reena is waiting for the same thing?
qa.a: Uma may feel surprised and a little relieved, realising the silence is shared fear rather than coldness from Reena.

grounding: A counsellor observes two partners each waiting for the other to move, stuck by pride and fear of another fight while distance grows.
